column4: REDAS: Capacity-building of Philippine Local Communities on the Use of REDAS Software
column5: Philippine Institute of Volcanology and Seismology
column6:
In 2002-2004, PHIVOLCS developed through a DOST-GIA grant, a software called REDAS (Rapid Earthquake Damage Assessment System).  The core REDAS software can simulate earthquake hazards such as ground shaking, liquefaction, landslides and tsunami.  Through the years, REDAS developed new capabilities including multi-hazard impact calculations and monitoring as well as database development in REDAS.  To do this, the REDAS Software Developer, Dr Bartolome C. Bautista, former Director of PHIVOLCS-DOST, put together existing database, algorithms, and freeware to create a software system.  Back in 2004, the original and initial modules of REDAS were a) simply plotting lines, points and polygons, b) viewing and sorting Philippine earthquake catalog and the c) Seismic Hazard Assessment (SHA) module.  In the SHA module, the user can simulate the earthquake intensity of a given earthquake scenario and plot them as peak ground acceleration (PGA) and intensity maps.  Through the years, other modules were developed.  To address the need of the local government units (LGUs) to acquire immediate earthquake and tsunami information, in 2008-2009, a module on Earthquake and Tsunami Alerting Module (ETAM) was developed and added in REDAS.  In this module, using internet connection, LGU Operation Centers can monitor automatically earthquake occurrences in near real time.  Users may opt to get their information from three sources such as PHIVOLCS, RIMES and USGS-NEIC. Users can also choose magnitude values that they want to be alerted on. Warning is issued via a speech synthesizer which can alert Watchstanders to the occurrence of earthquake and tsunami.  By 2010, another module, the REDAS Exposure Database Module (EDM) where LGUs can develop their own exposure database using a set of questionnaire and plot them on map was developed.  The REDAS EDM later on was placed in android smartphones as a collecting platform.  Also by this time, to make the REDAS software multi-hazard, hazard maps of hydrometeorological hazards such as floods, rain-induced landslides and storm surges are also incorporated into the software package when distributed. 
Around 2014, through various partnerships, PHIVOLCS was able to develop the impact assessment capabilities of REDAS.  Quantifying possible impacts will enable LGUs to prepare properly by having science-based estimate so potential losses in terms of lives and properties.  To do this, PHIVOLCS initially tapped the UPD ICE to develop engineering fragility curves for earthquakes.  The UPD ICE later developed curves for other hazards such as floods and severe wind hazards which are also incorporated in REDAS.  Following this development, through partnerships with SUCs in Regions II, III and XI, the REDAS SHAke module which can compute for impacts due to earthquakes was developed.  In the SHAke module, the user can compute possible earthquake impacts such as physical damage, fatalities and economic loss.  This is possible by combining earthquake hazard simulation, exposure data and fragility and vulnerability curves.   Then in 2016, in partnership with PAGASA and MGB, PHIVOLCS added two other impact calculation modules namely SWIFT (Severe Wind Impact Forecasting Tool) and FLoAT (Flood Loss Assessment Tool).  These additional impact assessment tools allow impact calculations for severe wind and flood hazards.  Post disaster surveys especially for earthquakes are done to gather data to further improve the engineering fragility curves in REDAS.   In 2017, PHIVOLCS co-developed the Crop Damage Assessment Tool (CropDAT), in cooperation with Region I SUCs.  In this module, impacts due to severe wind and floods can be computed for areas planted to agricultural crops like rice and corn.  The results are in terms of losses in yield and peso values.  The module was accompanied by a mobile application on data collection that can be used by LGUs for databasing their agricultural areas.  In 2019, the tsunami impact calculation module called TsuSIM (Tsunami Simulation and Impact calculation Module) was developed.  TsuSIM results are expressed in terms of the number of structures and persons affected.  Damages are categorized from None to Severe Damage and computed based on their building types.  In TsuSIM, users can plot tsunami hazard maps and from these, will be able to define their own tsunami evacuation routes and location of signages.  The TsuSIM is the module used by the REDAS Team to teach LGUs how to develop community-based tsunami early warning systems.  During the same year, the 2009 REDAS ETAM was refurbished to a new ETAM.  In this new ETAM, users can use Google Earth images to plot earthquakes aside from the usual earthquake monitoring.  The REDAS earthquake intensity reporting module called ToSIR (Tool for Seismic Intensity Reporting) is also incorporated in this module.  In ToSIR, REDAS users are able to report felt intensities whose results can help improve ground shaking simulation results. Also in 2019, the REDAS EDM was merged with the GeoMapperPH platform of PHIVOLCS’ GeoRiskPH  Project. In this REDAS EDM using GeoMapperPH module, the original EDM questionnaire was retained, with some additions on building attributes related to severe wind.  At the same time, the building location is collected as building polygon instead of data.  Data collection is also transmitted in real time via internet to a server.  In 2020, the latest REDAS module was developed which is the Satellite Rainfall Monitor (SRM). In SRM, the users may be able to tap international organizations like NOAA and JAXA to infer rainfall values in near real time.  SRM was developed because rain gauges are expensive and maintain and inherently difficult to install.  In SRM, users maybe able to install virtual rain gauges in any site of their choice. They can use this to monitor rain values and from these, develop local early warning systems for lahars, landslides and floods. In 2021, the REDAS Quick Lahar impacts Simulation Tool (QLIST) was developed. In QLIST, users can estimate impacts due to occurrence of volcanic lahars. QLIST is the first impact calculation method related to volcanic hazard. 
How is REDAS disseminated?
Due to high computer requirements to run simulations, running REDAS is done using individual computers.  Running it via web application is difficult considering the computer capabilities of users coupled with poor internet connectivity.  At the same time, the data required such as exposure database are not readily available and has to be developed by local communities.  With this situation, REDAS is shared through trainings where the software is installed in each participant’s laptops. The software distribution comes with a week-long training and post training support. This training and accompanying software provides savings for the country as software of similar kind and capabilities are expensive, hard-to-acquire and needs in-depth data preparation.  Since the onset of the Covid pandemic, the six-day training was segregated into modular online courses with Modules 1 and 2 being the stepping stone to higher modules specifically impact calculations modules such as SHAke, SWIFT, FLoAT, TsuSIM and CropDAT. 
REDAS was developed by PHIVOLCS and is now being shared to LGUs as a tool for emergency preparedness, contingency planning and more importantly for mainstreaming disaster risk reduction into the local development planning process. The software and training are free. Interested parties need to enter into a Memorandum of Agreement with PHIVOLCS in order to avail of the free software and training.  Despite the pandemic, for 2020, PHIVOCS has trained 380 participants from Zamboanga Sibugay, Lanao del Norte, Iligan City, OCD, JICA, Makati City, San Roque Power Corp., including Catholic Relief Services which supports the LGUs of Pasig, Caloocan, Manila, Pateros and San Jose del Monte City (Bulacan), etc.  For 2021, the target stakeholders are DSWD, Light Rail Management Corp., Nueva Vizcaya, Bulacan, Lanao del Norte, Iligan, and various state universities and colleges.  To date, PHIVOLCS has trained 56 provinces, 32 cities/municipalities, 44 state universities and colleges (SUCs), 79 private companies, 10 non-government organizations and seven government institutions on the use of the REDAS software.

column4: Enhancement of Volcano, Earthquake and Tsunami Warning Systems for Disaster Risk Reduction in the Philippines
column5: Philippine Institute of Volcanology and Seismology
column6:
The Japanese Government approved the funding of the  Grant Aid for the Project for Improvement of Equipment for Disaster Risk Management amounting to one billion Japanese Yen (Â¥1,000,000,000).   The PHIVOLCS project on Enhancement of Volcano, Earthquake and Tsunami Warning Systems for Disaster Reduction in the Philippines is one of the two projects under this Grant Aid.  (The other one is DPWH's Project on Disaster Mitigation Strengthening Tools). 
The PHIVOLCS project aims to efficiently provide fast and reliable earthquake, volcano and tsunami warning to the Office of Civil Defense, local government, media and the public.  The project involves the installation and maintenance of broadband seismometers, strong motion sensors, sea-level monitoring systems, and a network of intensity meters.   Ultimately it will enhance our real-time earthquake monitoring and tsunami warning system and an integrated real-time volcano monitoring.

column4: Geospatial Information Management
column5: National Mapping and Resource Information Authority
column6:
NAMRIA is mandated to integrate and manage geospatial data to facilitate access, analysis, and conversion into useful information. This project involves the buildup, integration, packaging, sharing, and dissemination of geospatial information utilizing information and communication technology (ICT) and geographic information system (GIS) technology.  The activities under this project include information systems strategic planning, geospatial database management, information systems development, and ICT infrastructure development. The project also provides for technical assistance, geomatics training, communication, education and public awareness, media relations and publications, promotions, marketing, and client services.

The agency currently maintains the Geoportal Philippines (GP) accessible at www.geoportal.gov.ph. It is an online platform that manages access and the open sharing of geospatial data holdings of NAMRIA and other stakeholders.  Currently, the GP hosts various thematic geospatial datasets on geohazards, forestry, mining, environment, road networks, health, and education, among others.

In carrying out its mandate, NAMRIA develops and maintains information systems to strengthen collaboration and data sharing among its technical branches.  These systems are NAMRIA Geospatial Information Management System/NAMRIA Geospatial, which serves as the NAMRIA node linked to the GP, and specific branch nodes connected to the NAMRIA node, namely, the Maritime Information System for hydrographic and marine datasets, the Environment and Natural Resources (ENR) Mapping Information System for ENR thematic datasets and the Topographic Mapping Information System for topographic and administrative datasets.
 
This project ensures continuous upgrades to hardware and the network.  It plays a vital role in improving NAMRIA’s delivery of geospatial information and services by reducing downtime, enhancing data management, and protecting crucial geospatial assets from imminent cyber threats.  

The agency continually strengthens its cybersecurity posture by implementing the Data Privacy Act (DPA), which includes establishing a Computer Emergency Response Team and enforcing strong access controls and encryption. Additionally, NAMRIA actively invests in Research and Development (R&D) to keep its systems resilient, aligns its operations with the National Cybersecurity Plan 2023-2028, and prioritizes the ongoing upgrading and maintenance of its critical ICT infrastructure—such as the GP—to eliminate vulnerabilities and ensure the reliable delivery of essential geospatial data for government planning and decision-making.

column4: Government Emergency Communications System (GECS)
column5: Department of Information and Communications Technology
column6:
An archipelagic country that is straddled along the Typhoon Belt, the
Philippines is prone to various natural disasters such as floods and cyclones. An
approximate of twenty (20) typhoons enter the country annually, many of
which are intense and destructive; implying that these events cause significant
losses of property, lives and livelihoods of Filipinos. Compounding the effects,
climate change worsens catastrophes due to human-induced urbanization,
deforestation and environmental degradation causing the escalation of climatic
elements like high temperatures, extreme rain, and intense gusts of wind,
among others. Although the Philippine disaster management has well
developed, the incessant occurrence of environmental crises still causes heavy
strain to the country in view of limited local resources and capacity. One of the
notable affected sectors is communications and connectivity; deemed an
integral component to be ensured during and immediately after a disaster
situation (i.e., in response and recovery). Connectivity is the ability to share
information amongst various groups within and outside of a disaster zone: the
government, responders, support organizations, community leaders, family
members, and the individual citizens. Thus, established communications amidst
calamities plays a vital role in community resilience. The GECS Project is the
Department’s solution to fulfill its mandate on disseminating vital information
through the use of ICT for disaster risk reduction and management.
(1) Provisioning of Mobile Operations Vehicle for Emergency (MOVE) Set
which is composed of the following:

a. Hub: A customized heavy-duty six-wheeler truck equipped with an
integrated communications system as a self-contained mobile operations and
coordination center through enabling wired and wireless connectivity for data
and voice communications to be used as a center of communication during
disasters and/or emergencies. This will be pre-positioned strategically to
provide backhaul links to both local and national command centers, including network access to the government agencies currently responding to any
emergency situation.
b. 4X4 Dispatch, a self-sustained connectivity hub installed in a heavy-duty
off-road vehicle that shall help widen the reach of the Hub into the disaster
zone to further extend the coverage for responders at ground zero; this may
provide video and image data to the Hub for cross-validation.
c. Motorcycle Dispatch, an off-road two-wheeled vehicle equipped with
communications equipment to support in reaching deeper into remote ground
inaccessible by the 4x4 Dispatch (e.g. mountain tops).
d. Drones, an unmanned aerial vehicle with a good range that further extends
the response range through high definition imagery to the ground in real-time
via fiber optic cable and a payload that can carry imaging equipment and
radios. Apart from the GECS MOVE, we provide Emergency ICT Equipment
with its Operations and Maintenance during disaster response depending on
the needs on ground.
The GECS Project aims to complete the service coverage to provide twenty (20)
GECS MOVE Sets and reach all seventeen (17) regions nationwide. It is
expected that there will be a dispatch augmentation with 1:3 Hub to Dispatch
ratio. The deployment plan per phase is based on the data from PAG-ASA on
the most frequently visited by a tropical cyclone per region per province.

column4: Hydrographic  and Oceanographic Surveys and Nautical Charting
column5: National Mapping and Resource Information Authority
column6:
The project involves the deployment of NAMRIA ships, launches, and small boats as platforms for conducting hydrographic surveys across the country’s maritime zones. The data gathered through these surveys are processed and used to produce nautical charts and other maritime publications essential for navigation and various maritime activities.

In addition, the project includes tide and tidal current observations, data processing, analysis, and prediction to generate tide and current tables for fisheries and maritime users. NAMRIA also establishes secondary and subordinate tide stations to enhance survey support and collects sea surface temperature, density, and salinity measurements to enrich the physical oceanographic data maintained at the National Oceanographic Data Center (NODC). The NODC provides critical oceanographic information needed for coastal development planning, climate change studies, and disaster risk management.

column4: Measurement Of Velocities of Earthquake Faults (MOVE Faults)
column5: Philippine Institute of Volcanology and Seismology
column6:
The successive earthquake events in Surigao on 10 Feb 2017 and in Leyte on 06 July 2017 underscore the importance of understanding the dynamics of crustal deformation and earthquake cycle processes. Although earthquake processes has never been fully understood, earthquake scientists do know that stress and strain accumulate around a fault where an earthquake will eventually be generated.  As widely accepted now, earthquake initiation normally starts when a large amount of strain energy is stored along the fault trace. In effect, the strain energy build up can be regarded as a preliminary process prior to an earthquake rupture. Close scrutiny of this preliminary process is therefore important for the long-term prediction of an earthquake. 

One of the powerful tools currently being used to monitor strain accumulation is the Global Positioning System (GPS). 

The use of GPS to study active faults in the Philippines is relatively new. It started in 1990s when PHIVOLCS, in collaboration with French researchers, used GPS to monitor crustal deformation along the Philippine Fault in Central Philippines. Since then, various foreign institutions (e.g. Indiana University, Academia Sinica of Taiwan, Kyoto Univesity) have been collaborating with PHIVOLCS to study the Philippine Fault and other active crustal structures in northern Luzon using this technology. One of the significant results of the use of GPS along the Philippine Fault is the recognition of a strain accumulation prior to the Ms 6.2  2003 February 16 Masbate earthquake (Bacolcol, 2003; 2005). This strain accumulation though was recognized only after the earthquake took place as it was the first time that a significant event occurred within the GPS networks of PHIVOLCS.  Nevertheless, these GPS campaign data gathered from mid 1990s to 2003 in Masbate proved that elastic strain accumulation along an active fault can be determined before a rupture can take place. Thus, if and when readily recognized, the crustal deformation patterns along an active fault trace as interpreted from GPS data can be an important tool in earthquake prediction.  Furthermore, horizontal displacements associated with the February 2017 and July 2017 in Surigao  and Leyte respectively were measured using GPS.

This project will monitor the crustal deformation along the active faults in the country.

column4: Metropolitan Manila Disaster Risk Reduction Management and Resiliency Program
column5: Metropolitan Manila Development Authority
column6: The Philippines is one of the most disaster-prone countries in the world due to its geographic location along the Pacific Ring of Fire and the typhoon belt of the Pacific Ocean. This exposes the country to frequent natural hazards, such as earthquakes, tsunamis, and typhoons, which have repeatedly resulted in significant human, economic, and environmental losses.  As the nation's political and economic center, Metro Manila is particularly vulnerable to these hazards due to its dense population, extensive built-up areas, and proximity to major seismic and coastal hazards. The West Valley Fault (WVF), part of the 100-kilometer Valley Fault System (VFS), runs through highly urbanized communities and is capable of generating a magnitude 7.2 earthquake. Meanwhile, the Manila Trench, located west of Luzon, is a major subduction zone with the potential to produce a magnitude 8.3 undersea earthquake capable of generating tsunamis ranging from 3.5 to 5.5 meters. Such an event could inundate low-lying coastal areas of Metro Manila. Beyond geological hazards, Metro Manila is also highly prone to hydrometeorological hazards, particularly typhoons, making Metro Manila prone to rapid flooding, infrastructure damage, and community displacement. Given these hazards, comprehensive disaster risk reduction and management strategies are essential for safeguarding communities and ensuring sustainable development across Metro Manila. The Disaster Risk Reduction Management and Resiliency Program utilizes scientific data, community-based approaches, and cross-sector collaboration to enhance preparedness, risk reduction, and resilience. Aligned with the Priority of the Sendai Framework, the program promotes strategic investments in resilient infrastructure, sustainable livelihoods, integration of risk reduction into urban planning, and capacity-building for institutions and communities. Importantly, the Metropolitan Manila Development Authority (MMDA) is an active member of the regional response during disasters, working closely with government agencies, LGUs, and partners to coordinate preparedness, emergency response, relief operations, and recovery activities.

column4: Operation Listo Program: DRRM-CCAM Institutional Capacity Enhancement for LGUs and DILG-LG Sector
column5: Local Government Academy
column6:
The Philippines is one of the hazard-prone countries due to its geographical location in the Pacific Ring of Fire and Typhoon Belt both for hydrometeorological and tectonic-geologic hazards. According to the Global Facility for Disaster Reduction and Recovery in 2017 as cited by the UN Office for Disaster Risk Reduction and Asian Disaster Preparedness, the country has at least 60% total land area that is susceptible to multiple hazards and 74% of the population exposed to the impact of these hazards. Given that the Philippines is a developing country, the effects of disasters may pose a great impact to the people but the gravity differs for low- and high-income countries.

Provided that the national government is aiming for zero casualty during disasters, the Local Government Units (LGUs) should align their DRR-CCA initiatives to the existing national policies and strengthen mechanisms to support these initiatives within their territorial jurisdictions.  Disasters can have serious implications for income inequality and persistence of poverty even as households adopt new risk diversification strategies in the aftermath of disasters (Jha et al., 2018, p. 22). According to them, “the capacity of households, businesses, and local communities to recover and restore livelihoods depends critically on the efficiency and effectiveness of post-disaster recovery and reconstruction efforts led by central and local governments” (p. 19). 

As the LGUs have strived to carry out the responsibility of responding to challenges on disaster operations and calamities,  Operation LISTO continues to be the flagship program of the Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG) through the Local Government Academy (LGA) on capacity development intervention for DRRM-CCAM.  The program shall continue to provide capacity building activities to local governments particularly on mainstreaming DRR-CCA in local development planning as LGUs have different levels of knowledge and/or understanding of implementing disaster risk reduction and climate change adaptation & mitigation actions, thus, leading to poor planning and implementation. 

The program provides a set of learning packages and knowledge products, workplace coaching assistance, support to Operation Centers nationwide and establishment of knowledge hubs to improve access of knowledge and information to advance DRRM & CCAM in the country.

column4: Palawan Environmentally Critical Areas Network (ECAN) Management Program
column5: Palawan Council for Sustainable Development Staff
column6: PCSD's 2026 proposal, coined as The Palawan Environmentally Critical Areas Network (ECAN) Management Program: Adapting in the New Normal towards a Secured and Sustainable Future, shall bring to the existing programs/projects/activities of the PCSD under the Palawan Environmentally Critical Areas Network (ECAN) Management Program, technologies and innovations from best practices of environment and natural resources management. This is to attain a healthy and fully functioning environment that ensures a continuous flow of ecosystem services for a robust economy, and the protection and improvement of human welfare. These include innovations in decision support tools generated from the World Bank funded projects such as Capturing Coral Reef and Related Ecosystem Services (CCRES) and the Wealth Accounting and Valuation of Ecosystem Services (WAVES); USAID funded innovative management from the Strengthening the Marine Protected Areas to Conserve Marine Key Biodiversity Areas in the Philippines (SMARTSEAS) Project, Fish Right Program, Protect Wildlife Project, Philippine Sustainable Interventions for Biodiversity, Oceans, and Landscapes (SIBOL) Project; Forest Foundation Philippines (FFP), among others. Furthermore, the proposed expansion will include new researches for management and policy, and innovative education strategies.

column4: All Weather Communication
column5: Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration
column6:
With the continuous increase in demand for faster and more reliable connectivity to enhance the agency's system performance and user experience, it has become necessary to improve the existing network security infrastructure. column4: Installation of High Frequency Radars At Coastal Areas
column5: Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration
column6:
PAGASA’s existing HF oceanographic radar network was designed to provide such data, yet several key sites are no longer operational. Restoring and expanding coverage in San Bernardino Strait, Verde Island Passage, and Surigao Strait is both urgent and strategic.

San Bernardino Strait (Matnog-Allen) - A major maritime gateway linking the Pacific Ocean with the central Philippine seas, frequently traversed by inter-island and international vessels. Its strong currents and exposure to typhoons make it a high-risk navigation zone requiring continuous monitoring.

Verde Island Passage (Calapan-Batangas) - Known as the "center of the center" of maritime biodiversity and a critical shipping lane between Luzon and the Visayas. Monitoring here safeguards both maritime traffic and the ecological integrity that underpins fisheries, tourism, and local livelihoods.

Surigao Strait (San Ricardo-San Francisco) - The primary sea route between the Visayas and Mindanao, heavily railed upon for domestic trade and inter-island transport. Its tidal dynamics and vulnerability to weather extremes heighten the need for reliable observation data.

In order to address the observational requirements of these critical and high-traffic maritime corridors, existing High Frequency Radar (HFR) systems will be redeployed from other locations, with corresponding rehabilitation works and re-establishment of station infrastructure to ensure full operational functionality.

column4: Observing Facilities and Equipment Maintenance Program
column5: Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration
column6:
The repair, rehabilitation, and upgrading of PAGASA's observing facilities are critical to strengthening the vital country's meteorological infrastructure. The restoration of damage weather stations ensures continuity of ground-based observations, while the replacement and upgrading of basic instruments in synoptic and agromet stations improve the accuracy of forecasts vital for aviation, agriculture, and disaster rick reduction. The operation and maintenance of the weather surveillance radar network provide real-time monitoring of severe weather system, reinforcing the early warning capacity of the agency. Furthermore, the replacement and upkeep of automatic weather stations safeguard uninterrupted automated data collection for local forecasting and climate services. The rehabilitation and upgrading of automated weather observation systems sustain aviation safety and compliance with international civil aviation standards.

Continuity of weather forecasting and public warnings depends on safe, compliant, and reliable facilities. Current conditions - aging structures, undocumented/legacy installations, and systems requiring re-analysis-pose risks to safety, uptime, and regulatory compliance. The project addresses these gaps through: (a) field measurements and materials/soil testing (coring, rebound, GPR, boreholes); (b) structural and MEPF re-analysis per NSCP and applicable code; (c) system performance tests for power/lightning, AC & ventilation, fire sprinkler/FDAS, CCTV/ICT; (d) preparation of as-built plans, design reports, technical specifications, BoQ/cost estimates, and an IFC BIM; and (e) permit facilitation. By embedding energy-efficiency (EEC Act, GEMP/AO 11) and green site strategies (cool roofs/daylighting where feasible, native landscaping, drainage/stormwater improvements), the program reduces operating cost and environment footprint while improving comfort, accessibility, and safety. The resulting compliance, documentation, and upgrade roadmap directly support uninterrupted PAGASA operations and resilient service delivery nationwide. Finally, the replacement and maintenance of hydrogen generators for upper-air stations are indispensable to ensure the continuity of upper-air soundings, which supply critical data for global and regional national observing network, enabling PAGASA to deliver accurate, timely, and science-based information for disaster preparedness, public safety, and climate resilience.

column4: Doppler Weather Radar Enhancement Project
column5: Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration
column6:
MACTAN-CEBU WEATHER RADAR 
Given the radar’s more than seven (7) years of continuous operation and the increasing frequency of mechanical failures and electronic component breakdowns, the system is now affected by the obsolescence of key parts—particularly the transmitter units, which are no longer available in the market. The unavailability of these critical components poses a significant risk to sustained radar operations and to PAGASA’s ability to deliver essential weather and flood warning services. In view of these conditions, it is strongly recommended to replace the entire radar system to ensure reliable, accurate, and uninterrupted meteorological observations and to support PAGASA’s mandate in hazard monitoring and public safety.

GUIUAN WEATHER RADAR 
The Guiuan weather radar station in Eastern Samar plays a critical role in monitoring typhoons entering the Philippines from the east, as well as weather conditions across the Visayas and northern Mindanao. Completed in 2013 through JICA funding, it is one of the country’s first S-Band radars to use a solid-state power amplifier (SSPA) instead of a magnetron transmitter. The radar has been instrumental in tracking major typhoons and supporting PAGASA’s forecasts on storm position, wind speed, and rainfall. In recent years, however, the system has suffered major failures and prolonged downtime due to wear and tear. Restoration has become increasingly difficult because the manufacturer has stopped producing S-Band solid-state radars, leaving essential replacement parts unavailable.

ZAMBOANGA, QUEZON (PALAWAN), AND BUSUANGA WEATHER RADARS 
The weather radars in Zamboanga (established July 1, 2016), Quezon, Palawan (established January 15, 2015), and Busuanga (established January 17, 2018) have all been in continuous operation for several years and are now exhibiting visible signs of deterioration. As these systems age, their components become increasingly prone to failure, resulting in more frequent downtime and reduced operational reliability. Within the next five years, these radars are expected to require significantly higher maintenance efforts and costs, particularly due to aging electronic parts, mechanical wear, and the growing difficulty in sourcing compatible replacement components. Continued operation under these conditions may lead to extended outages that compromise the effectiveness of PAGASA’s weather monitoring and warning services. In order to ensure sustained, accurate, and reliable radar coverage—especially in regions frequently affected by severe weather—it is strongly recommended to initiate the replacement of these radar systems before maintenance becomes excessively difficult and cost-inefficient.

column4: Development of an Interactive El Niño Response Matrix tool (ERMat) to trigger early action for drought
column5: Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration
column6: Over the last two decades, the Philippines has been heavily impacted by drought due to El Niño.  It is more difficult to anticipate the rainfall necessary to make the more important crop production decisions, and water resources management and complicates other form of drought adaptations.  Reliable forecasts of  El Niño Southern Oscillation (ENSO), El Niño in particular, would allow a clear set of early warning protocols needed to trigger when the different national or agency-specific level or local level mobilizes its ENSO response mechanisms.  For example, the local governments could establish the severity or certainty threshold for a forecasted ENSO event to ensure the local El Niño Team is reconstituted with sufficient lead time to enact response measures, Therefore, there is a need to develop and provide an ENSO response tool, to help prepare for El Niño through their ability to trigger early actions before drought impacts develop. National and Local Climate Change Expenditure Tagging (CCET) through DBM-CCC Joint Memo Circular 2015-01 and DBM-CCC-DILG JMC 2015-01 require all levels of National Government Agencies (NGAs), State Universities and Colleges (SUCs), Government Owned- and Controlled-Corporations (GOCCs) and Local Government Units (LGUs) to tag climate change-related programs/projects/activities in their budgets and Annual Investment Plans (AIPs).

During the budget preparation phase, concerned National Government Instrumentalities  (NGIs) are required to submit their climate-tagged programs/activities/projects (PAPs) through the Quality Assurance and Review (QAR) Form to the CCC.

The CCC, through the CCET Helpdesk, performs the following functions: 
- monitors, tracks, and evaluates climate change budget proposals identified by NGIs; 
- assists NGIs, through capacity building and technical assistance on how they can identify climate PAPs in their regular budgets; and 
- issues quality assurance approval to agencies on the alignment of budget proposals to climate change thematic priorities. 

In addition, the CCC is responsible for screening and recommending PAPs aligned with the National Climate Change Action Plan. PAPs that aim to address geological or human-induced disasters are not recommended in the climate budget proposals of agencies. 

Once cleared and approved by the CCC, these climate-tagged PAPs will be recommended to the DBM for inclusion in the climate budget allocation. PAPs not endorsed by the CCC may still be budgeted but not climate-tagged. 

Upon the release of the National Expenditure Program (NEP) and the approval of the General Appropriations Act (GAA), the CCC issues climate budget briefs to report the climate PAPs approved in the GAA. The CCC continues to monitor the climate-tagged PAPs throughout each budget phase.

The Local CCET In line with the Rationalized Planning System, local governments must assess, identify, and tag thier climate change PPAs and bugdet, during the planning and budgeting process, in the Annual Invetsment Programs (AIPs). Meanwhile, the CCC provided technical support, conducts the quality assessment review of the submissions, and monitors the tagged PAPs and their budget based on their AIP submissions.

Furthermore, the CCC is responsible for the following functions:
- Monitor and evaluate PAPs of local government units tagged as climate change responsive and craft technical analysis on the matter;
- To inform policy-and decision-making based on findings of the M&E cycle and and fucntional adaptation and mitigation typologies;
- To build local governments' capacity on climate change expenditure tagging; and
- To provide technical advisory and assistance to local government units on matters relating to tagging CC PPAs and related CC plan/program mainstreaming matters

column4: Fishery Interventions and Stewardship for Healthy Marine Ecosystems (FISHME)
column5: Surigao del Norte State University
column6:
The Municipality of Malimono, Surigao del Norte is endowed with abundant marine and coastal resources owing to its productive waters along the Bohol Sea. These waters significantly contribute to the fish supply of the province and nearby areas, supporting a wide range of marine species such as sardines, anchovies, tuna, mollusks, abalones, and other shellfishes. The richness of these resources is closely linked to the presence of coral reefs, diverse coastal geomorphology, and varied substrates such as sand, gravel, pebbles, and rock formations that serve as natural habitats for marine vertebrates and invertebrates.

Despite this natural abundance, coastal and marine ecosystems face increasing threats from illegal and destructive fishing practices, weak enforcement of fisheries laws, and limited community awareness and participation in resource management. While the Philippines has comprehensive legal and policy frameworks for coastal and marine resource protection, effective implementation remains a challenge due to the technical, procedural, and tactical complexity of coastal law enforcement. Addressing these issues requires not only enforcement of national fisheries laws but also the formulation and implementation of responsive municipal ordinances, strengthened Marine Protected Areas (MPAs), and a shift from open-access fisheries toward regulated and sustainable management systems.

The FISHME Component is designed as an integrated extension and capacity-building initiative that responds to these challenges through education, stewardship, and participatory governance. The program emphasizes the use of biophysical science tools and methodologies to establish baseline ecological conditions and monitor trends in marine ecosystems. These scientific approaches provide critical information for evidence-based decision-making, particularly in the design, management, and evaluation of MPAs and fish sanctuaries. By enhancing local capacity in ecological monitoring and fisheries assessment, the program supports adaptive management practices that contribute to biodiversity conservation, food security, and climate resilience.

A key feature of the FISHME Component is its strong focus on community participation and ownership. The program recognizes that effective marine conservation cannot be sustained without the active involvement and commitment of local stakeholders. Through Information, Education, and Communication (IEC) campaigns, skills training, and participatory workshops, the program aims to build a strong local constituency that supports fish sanctuaries and marine conservation initiatives. These efforts help ensure compliance with management rules, continuity of conservation efforts amid political changes, and shared responsibility for enforcement and maintenance activities such as patrols and installation of marker buoys.

The FISHME Component also integrates gender-responsive approaches in line with the Magna Carta of Women, recognizing the critical but often undervalued role of women in fisheries, food security, and household nutrition. The program addresses gender disparities in access to resources, participation in decision-making, and economic opportunities by promoting gender awareness among fisheries officers, local government personnel, and community members. It seeks to enhance the visibility, empowerment, and inclusion of women in fisheries organizations, livelihood activities, and development planning processes.

Surigao del Norte State University (SNSU), particularly its Malimono Campus through the BS Marine Biology and BS Fisheries programs, serves as a key implementing partner of the FISHME Component. In fulfillment of its mandate to contribute to the development and conservation of marine and fishery resources, SNSU provides technical expertise, research-based inputs, and training support. The university’s involvement strengthens the linkage between science, policy, and community action, ensuring that conservation and fisheries management initiatives are grounded in sound scientific principles and inclusive development practices.

Overall, the FISHME Component aims to enhance sustainable fisheries management, protect and rehabilitate marine ecosystems, promote gender equity, and improve food security and livelihoods in coastal communities. By combining scientific knowledge, community stewardship, institutional capacity-building, and participatory governance, the program contributes to healthier marine ecosystems and an improved quality of life for present and future generations in Malimono, Surigao del Norte.

column6: Marine toxins threaten the health of the oceans and pose threats to the marine biota and humans. column4: Supporting our seas through automated and integrated networks (SUSTAIN): Strengthening ocean observation and management risks to coastal ecosystems. Project 3. Cultivating people-centered risk knowledge building with coastal communities through citizen science
column5: Philippine Council for Agriculture, Aquatic and Natural Resources Research and Development
column6:
Coastal communities and small-scale fishers in the Philippines continually face worsening coastal challenges such as dwindling fish catch, habitat disruption, and toxic blooms that severely threaten food production, livelihoods, and income. These are affected by multiple hazards and drivers such as loss of biodiversity, environmental degradation and pollution, and climate-change-related phenomena such as sea level rise. Despite these occurrences, there are pronounced gaps in systematizing the risk knowledge of these coastal threats. At the same time, dominant risk management approaches disregard community capacities and responses with top-down strategies. While the trend for citizen science practice worldwide grows, there is still a need to reinforce citizen science models that give more access to local people in defining problems, designing research, as well as analyzing and utilizing information for appropriate actions.

This proposed project aims to initiate community-based risk knowledge-building to contribute to effective risk management of coastal threats, through the process of community-scientists co-creation. This can be achieved by increasing the community’s self-assessment capacities; initiating a community-based monitoring mechanism for coastal ecosystem parameters; and developing response plans for coastal ecosystem risks.

column4: A Coupled Digital Twin and Urban Climate Modelling System for Smart and Resilient Urban Environments

column6:
Urban areas are particularly vulnerable to climate change due to dense populations, concentrated infrastructure, and interactions between natural and built environments. Challenges include heat waves, flooding, water stress, poor air quality, extreme weather, and infrastructure and health risks. Addressing these requires high-resolution urban climate data beyond the scope of current observation networks and large-scale climate models.

Urban digital twins are virtual city models built from sensor data, satellite imagery, and demographics. These models simulate urban environments in real-time, supporting urban planning, infrastructure management, disaster response, and sustainability efforts. They enable planners to test scenarios, optimize systems, and enhance resilience.

In urban climate modeling, 3D city models from digital twins provide detailed representations of urban areas, critical for understanding local climate dynamics. They help quantify the urban heat island effect, simulate air and heat flow, and assess the impact of urban design on climate, enabling the development of sustainable and adaptive urban strategies.

column4: Enhancing Civil Aviation Safety through a Low-Level Wind Shear Surveillance and Warning System at the Ninoy Aquino International Airport
column5: Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration
column6:
Low-level wind shear is a critical meteorological phenomenon that can significantly affect the safety and performance of an aircraft, especially during critical phases of flight such as take-off, initial climb, approach. and landing. Despite the prevalence of LLWS occurrences in domestic and international aerodromes in the country based on pilot reports from the Civil Aviation Authority of the Philippines, the country has yet establish and implement a real-time surveillance and warning system for LLWS at NAIA or any aerodrome in the country. This stems from, among other reasons, the lack of advanced aerodromes meteorological equipment such as LLWS alerting system, terminal Doppler weather radar, and scanning Doppler lidar to detect low-level wind shear in real time. With information on LLWS only coming from pilot reports, this situation places a strain on safety protocols and operational efficiency, resulting in flight delays, cancellations, and even potential safety risk to both passenger and flight crew.

As the designated aeronautical meteorological service provider, the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Administration (DOST-PAGASA) through the Aeronautical Meteorological Services Section is tasked under the Philippine Civil Aviation Regulations and civil aviation regulations and standards of the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) to provide wind shear warnings to aerodromes to ensure safety of flight operations and improve operational efficiency. In line with its mandate under the law and crucial to the effective implementation of its task, there is a pressing need for DOST-PAGASA to establish a real-time surveillance and warning system for low-level wind shear at NAIA, thereby enhancing safety and minimizing the economic impact caused by weather-related incidents. This includes the installation of low-level wind shear alerting system, terminal Doppler weather radar, and scanning Doppler lidar, as well as the capacity building of PAGASA aeronautical meteorologists to implement the system in coordination with relevant air traffic units of Civil Aviation Authority of the Philippines

column4: Operational Ocean Modelling for Marine Service Applications

column6:
Ocean hydrodynamic modelling is an essential component of operational oceanographic services due to its ability to provide

As an archipelagic maritime nation with a growing maritime industry and blue economy, the Philippines is highly dependent on timely, accurate, and reliable prediction of physical oceanographic conditions (i.e., waves, currents, salinity, sea surface temperature, tide heights) to ensure safety of navigation, support marine emergency response, and promote the efficiency and productivity of transportation, logistics, fisheries, and other marine economic activities. These prediction of these parameters can only be achieved through the implementation of an operational ocean forecast system that provides high-resolution model simulations, with provision of data assimilation.

In line with its role as the marine meteorological service and as prescribe in applicable WMO technical regulations and national policies (e.g., National Oil Spill Contingency Plan/NPSCP), the Weather Division - Maritime Meteorological Service Section (WD-MMSS) of PAGASA provides services to support the conduct of marine environmental emergency response (MEER; e.g., during spills of oil and HNS and in radionuclide dispersion incidents) and maritime search and rescue (SAR) of relevant national response agencies (e.g., Philippine Coast Guard). Furthermore, the portfolio of future product of the WD-MMSS include the provision of ship voyage optimization service for vessel operating or transiting within the maritime jurisdiction of the country. These highly specialized services require the operation of spill trajectory and fate model (MEER), object drift models (for SAR), and ship weather routeing model - all requiring geophysical forcing from an operational ocean hydrodynamic model. At present, neither the ocean hydrodynamic model nor the three (3) specialized models is operated by PAGASA

Given the growing demand for the above mentioned specialized services and following the operational experiences during the MT Terranova incident and various maritime SAR operations which required the support services from PAGASA, there is a pressing need not only to implement the downstream models for MEER, maritime SAR, and ship weather routeing, but also establish the technical and hardware capability to perform high resolution regional ocean modelling.

column4: Watershed Characterization and Vulnerability Assessment (WCVA) for Priority River Watersheds in Region IX

The project involves the comprehensive characterization and assessment of the seven (7)
priority river watersheds (RW) in Region IX, namely: (a) Quipit RW; (b) Labason RW; (c) Rebocon RW; (d) Surabay RW; (e) Sindangan RW; (f) Lituban RW; and (g) Palandok RW, to determine their physical, biological, socio-economic, and institutional conditions. The following are the profile is the seven priority river watersheds in Region IX:
a. Quipit River Watershed has a total area of 72,097.67 ha with covering areas within the

column4: Land Management and Governance
column5: Department of Environment and Natural Resources
column6:
The program integrates three major activities of the Land Sector: land surveys, land disposition and management, and land records management (approved by DBM for 2014).  The above-mentioned major activities are interdependent, complementary, and cyclical.  To illustrate, no public land can be disposed of through any mode of disposition without an approved survey.  In turn, the need for surveys depends on the demand for and magnitude of land for disposition and management.  Land claims and conflicts invariably require that the disputed properties be surveyed before they can be properly adjudicated.  Land records generated from these activities must be secured, preserved, and properly stored.  Efficient records management highly facilitates land surveys and mapping as well as land disposition and management.

Land Administration involves activities related to Surveys, Titling and Records and Systems Management. This also includes the implementation of the Land Administration and Management Philippines (LAMS-Phil.) which resulted in improved access to land records and information at reduced costs to the government, private and public clients, faster delivery of land-related services, and subsequently increased land-related transactions. 
This program also strengthens institutional capacity and inter-agency coordination to drive evidence-based policy reforms and improve land governance, accelerate the massive titling of government lands to address PDP shortfalls and enhance efficient land utilization, promote inclusive land administration by increasing transparency, public participation, and equitable access to land resources.
A systematic adjudication process is adopted to minimize, if not eliminate, the risk of issuing patents to spurious individuals other than the qualified beneficiary. Under the systematic adjudication process, which was developed under the Land Administration and Management Program 2 (LAMP2), the involvement of the community was adopted in the determination of land rights, identification of beneficiaries, and defining parcel boundaries of the land. Likewise, the assistance by the LGUs as partners in the titling process will result in clear understanding among the people of the land disposition service of the DENR and, at the same time, complement the manpower of the Land Management Sector.
Rapid Land Tenure Appraisal is also institutionalized. It is an activity that focuses on the untitled lots to determine the potential lots before titling operations are entered into. The result of this activity shall be used to prioritize barangays based on the number of workable lots
Land Management focuses more on the use and stewardship of land resources. This includes activities such as the Management of Foreshore Areas, Government-Owned Lands and Administering lands that are owned by the government including patrimonial properties. This program also focuses on key investment areas to boost revenue and support climate adaptation, while improving land valuation and asset management to maximize economic and social benefits, utilize modern technology like geospatial mapping and digital tools to enhance data accuracy and strengthen land administration systems and ensure fair conflict resolution and promote sustainable land management practices for long-term resource efficiency.

Land surveys & mapping refers to all activities related to the identification, delineation, and mapping of agricultural lands of the public domain and all other government lands and properties under the jurisdiction of DENR.  It embraces cadastral surveys, field network surveys, and all other types of surveys undertaken by the sector. Land disposition and management involves all activities related to the processing, approval, and issuance of concessions (homestead for agricultural lands and free patent for agricultural & residential lands) involving public lands in favor of qualified individuals; investigation and resolution of land cases; titling of untitled government properties as well. Covers issuance of patents in public residential and agricultural lands under RA 10023 (otherwise known as “An act authorizing the issuance of Free Patents to Residential Lands”) and RA 6657 (otherwise known as the Comprehensive Agrarian Reform Law of 1988), respectively.

Land Records management pertains to all activities related to receiving, releasing, classifying, filing or retrieval of land records.  These include survey records, public land records, and legal records. The Land Administration and Management System (LAMS) was developed to effectively manage the DENR Land Records and related services; it will cover completing the data build-up and conversion to Digital format. LAMS also includes data capture and Digital Cadastral Database (DCDB) Cleansing to streamline and secure the land administration process.

column4: Geo-Referenced Mapping of Landslide-Prone Residential Zones for Community Awareness
column5: Surigao del Norte State University
column6:
The Geo-Referenced Mapping of Landslide-Prone Residential Zones for Community Awareness project is designed to identify, assess, and map residential areas susceptible to landslides in selected barangays of Surigao del Norte. Using geo-referenced field surveys, geographic information systems (GIS), and spatial analysis, the project generates scientifically validated landslide susceptibility maps that clearly indicate areas at varying levels of risk.

The project aims to translate technical hazard assessment into community-friendly information products that can be easily understood and utilized by households, barangay officials, and local disaster risk reduction and management (DRRM) committees. Through the production of hazard maps, awareness materials, and barangay briefings, the initiative strengthens local preparedness and supports informed decision-making related to land use, settlement safety, and disaster mitigation.

This initiative is jointly implemented by the Surigao del Norte State University – Civil Engineering Department, Mines and Geosciences Bureau (MGB) Caraga Region XIII, and collaborating local government units. By integrating academic expertise, government technical support, and local knowledge, the project contributes to risk-informed community planning, reduced disaster vulnerability, and improved resilience of residential areas against landslide hazards.

column4: National Volcano, Earthquake and Tsunami Monitoring and Warning Center
column5: Philippine Institute of Volcanology and Seismology
column6:
The PHIVOLCS National Volcano, Earthquake, and Tsunami Monitoring and Warning Center will serve as the primary hub for the country’s disaster monitoring efforts. Currently, the Philippines faces constant threats from geological hazards; this project creates a single, high-tech location where all data from across the country is collected and analyzed 24/7.

The facility will be equipped with a centralized Operations Center, where experts use specialized software to monitor ground movements and sea levels in real-time. By bringing all monitoring tools under one roof, the center removes delays in communication. This means that as soon as a threat is detected, the center can immediately send out alerts to local governments and the general public.

To ensure the center never fails during an emergency, the building itself will be built with extra-strong foundations and its own back-up power and satellite systems. This ensures that even if a major earthquake causes a blackout or knocks out phone lines, the center will stay online to guide the nation.

column6:
A Nature Study Park/ Mangrove Eco-Park, like the Katunggan Eco-park in Iloilo, offers a variety of benefits. It can serve as a long-term solution to flooding, acting as a natural buffer against strong winds and waves, and protecting shorelines. These parks can also provide livelihood and income generation opportunities for local communities through ecotourism and related activities. Additionally, they play a crucial role in promoting ecotourism, raising environmental awareness, and supporting biodiversity conservation. 
The proposed budget will be used for the establishment of nature study park/Eco park in Iloilo City located at Brgy. Hinactacan, Lapaz,  Iloilo City. The project is being proposed by Local  Government  of Iloilo city since 2017 represented by Honorable Mayor Jerry Treñas and Congresswoman Juliene Baronda of the Local Congressional District of Iloilo. It has a total  area of 35 has. Mangrove forest. The said area was already assessed in 2015 under USAID. The results showed there is a high species richness of 15 true mangroves species in the Philippines while results of the initial Biomass and Carbon  Stock Assessment showed that the overall total mean biomass was 120.03 ton/ha with  equivalents of 55.60 ton/hap C and 204.06 ton/haCO2. The total value for biomass was 4,209.55 tons with equivalents of 1,949.96 ton C and 7,156.35 ton CO2, much higher than any of  the sampling site. Hence, this proposal to establish the Hinactan Mangrove Eco-park and  Learning Center is recognized to be crucial for the protection and sustainable development of  the mangrove ecosystem in Iloilo City.

column4: Enhancing Earthquake Resilience through Advanced Mapping of Safe Open Spaces and Critical Lifeline Facilities in the Greater Metro Manila Area and Other High-Risk Areas in the Philippines
column5: National Mapping and Resource Information Authority
column6:
The project aims to strengthen urban resilience by providing updated and accurate geospatial data for earthquake preparedness and response.
       Metro Manila and adjacent provinces along the valley fault system face the looming threat of a magnitude 7.2 earthquake, "The Big One", which could cause massive destruction, displacement, and disruption of essential services.  From 2021 to 2022, NAMRIA validated 6,652 SOS sites in Metro Manila, but rapid urbanization has rendered many outdated or unusable.
      Building on the "Quadrant Mapping" initiative, the project will update Metro Manila's SOS maps amd expand coverage to vulnerable provinces and other high-risk areas nationwide - ensuring coordinated disaster preparedness and response across urban and rural communities.  SOS are hazard-free zones serving as evacuation sites, temporary shelters, and operational hubs, while integrated CLF mapping will strengthen LGU contingency planning, inter-agency coordination, and public awareness.
      Regularly updating SOS datasets ensures accuracy, accessibility, and relevance, supporting effective evacuation planning, emergency response, and long-term urban resilience.  Outputs will be accessible via the Geoportal Philippines, aligned with SDGs 11, 13, and 17, and the PDP 2023-2028, promoting risk-informed geospatially driven decision-making for safer, more resilient communities.

column4: Development of a Watershed Health Monitoring System for Selected Proclaimed Watershed Reservations in the Philippines
column5: Department of Environment and Natural Resources
column6:
Proclaimed watershed reservations in the Philippines are strategically designated areas that play a critical role in ensuring national water security, environmental sustainability, and climate resilience.

These watersheds are primarily established to protect, maintain, and enhance water yield for domestic supply, agricultural irrigation, and hydropower generation, while regulating land use and preventing forest exploitation and degradation. As such, proclaimed watershed reservations directly support the country's long-term development objectives by securing reliable water resources that support economic productivity, public health, and energy security. (PD 705, s.1975)

A key foundation of effective watershed management is the establishment and assessment of watershed or ecosystem health. Watershed health is defined as the combined outcome of sound management interventions and the application of integrative ecological science (Rapport et al., 1998). It provides a systematic and holistic framework for evaluating watershed conditions using
multiple indicators, including those related to the natural environment, hydrology, and
aquatic ecology (Ahn & Kim, 2017). This indicator-based approach enables managers
to better understand complex watershed-ecosystem interactions and supports adaptive and iterative
decision-making processes consistent with integrated watershed management principles.
At present, however, a comprehensive and institutionalized watershed health monitoring
system based on this integrative framework is largely absent in proclaimed watershed reservations in the Philippines. The lack of continuous, standardized, and science-driven monitoring limits the ability of management authorities to assess watershed conditions, evaluate the effectiveness of interventions, and respond proactively to emerging pressures arising from land-use change, population growth, and climate variability. Addressing this gap is critical to strengthening evidence-based planning, policy formulation, and investment prioritization. This proposal seeks to develop a Watershed Health Monitoring System for selected proclaimed watershed reservations in the Philippines. The proposed system aims to generate timely, reliable, and policy-relevant information on key watershed health indicators to support informed decision-making, improved management
strategies, and adaptive governance. By strengthening institutional capacity for monitoring and assessment, the project will contribute directly to the achievement of the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), particularly SDG 6 (Clean Water and Sanitation), SDG 11 (Sustainable Cities and
Communities), and SDG 13 (Climate Action), while reinforcing national objectives on water security, climate resilience, and sustainable natural resource management as articulated in the Philippine Development Plan and related sectoral frameworks.
